questions.q: Why doesn't Lesson 23's iteration cap, by itself, bound how expensive or how broad an agent's run can get?
options: An iteration cap already guarantees a fixed cost and scope for every task
A fixed number of iterations can still vary hugely in cost (cheap lookups vs. expensive calls) and in how much the agent touches, so cost and scope need their own separate limits
Iteration caps have been deprecated in favor of cost limits
Iteration caps only apply to approval checkpoints, not to cost
questions.explain: Fifteen iterations of a cheap tool costs little, while fifteen iterations involving expensive calls or broad data access can be costly or wide-reaching even while staying under the same step count — iteration count alone doesn't capture that.

questions.q: How can a running token/API cost budget be tracked accurately rather than estimated?
options: By asking the model to self-report how much it thinks it has spent
By using the real usage data (input and output token counts) included in every Claude API response to compute actual spend after each call
Cost cannot be tracked at all during a running agent loop
By counting only the number of tool calls made, regardless of token volume
questions.explain: Every API response includes real usage data, so accumulating spend from input_tokens and output_tokens after each response gives an exact running total rather than a guess.

questions.q: What does an action-scope limit like "MAX_RECORDS_MODIFIED = 1" guard against that a cost budget does not?
options: It prevents the agent from ever calling more than one tool in total
It bounds the blast radius of a mistake directly — how much the agent can touch — independent of how cheap or expensive those actions were in tokens
It has the exact same effect as a cost budget and is redundant with it
It only matters for agents that never modify any data
questions.explain: A record-touch limit caps how much the agent can affect regardless of token cost, which is why it's described as one of the highest-leverage guardrails for agents that modify data — a cheap mistake can still touch many records without it.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say cost and action-scope budgets should be enforced in application code around the loop, rather than as instructions in the system prompt?
options: System prompts are not capable of containing any text about budgets
A prompt instruction is only a suggestion the model might not follow under pressure, while a code-level check before each tool execution is a guarantee that actually stops execution
Code-level checks are slower than prompt instructions, so they should be avoided
The Claude API automatically enforces any budget mentioned in the system prompt
questions.explain: Asking the model to "stay within budget" in the prompt relies on the model's compliance; a hard check enforced by your own code before executing a tool call cannot be talked past the way a prompt instruction can.

questions.q: What should happen when an agent's cost or action-scope budget is exhausted in the middle of a task?
options: The task should crash with no explanation of what happened
The budget should be silently doubled so the agent can keep going unnoticed
The loop should stop as a defined stopping point, reporting what was completed versus what wasn't, so a human can decide whether to raise the budget or narrow the scope
The agent should ignore the budget and continue anyway since the task isn't finished
questions.explain: Running out of budget mid-task is treated the same way as Lesson 23's stopping conditions: a clean, reported stop rather than a silent failure, leaving the decision to extend or rescope the task to a human.
